title: Electric Potential
summary: Electric potential $V$ is potential energy per unit charge, measured in volts. For a point charge $V = k\dfrac{q}{r}$ (a scalar — no direction). Moving a charge through a potential difference does work $W = q\,\Delta V$, and in a uniform field $V = Ed$. (University Physics Vol. 2, Ch. 7.)

concept_sections.heading: Potential = energy per charge
concept_sections.explanation: Electric potential at a point is the potential energy a charge would have there, per coulomb: $V = U/q$. Its unit is the volt (1 V = 1 J/C). Potential difference $\Delta V$ between two points is what a battery or power supply provides. Unlike field, potential is a scalar — just a number, no direction.

figure.caption: Potential is like height: the energy each coulomb carries, $V = U/q$ (1 V = 1 J/C).

concept_sections.heading: Potential of a point charge
concept_sections.explanation: A point charge sets up a potential $V = k\dfrac{q}{r}$ around it, taking $V = 0$ at infinity. It is positive near positive charge and negative near negative charge. Because it is a scalar, the potential from several charges is a simple sum $V = \sum k\dfrac{q_i}{r_i}$ — no components needed.

figure.caption: Concentric equipotentials around a point charge; $V$ falls off as $1/r$ (V → 0 at ∞).

concept_sections.heading: Work and energy
concept_sections.explanation: Moving a charge $q$ through a potential difference $\Delta V$ takes work $W = q\,\Delta V$, and its potential energy changes by $\Delta U = q\,\Delta V$. If only the electric force acts, energy is conserved: a charge speeds up as it moves to lower potential energy, $q\,\Delta V = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

figure.caption: A charge accelerated across a potential difference gains kinetic energy: $W = q\,\Delta V = \tfrac12 mv^2$.

concept_sections.heading: Field and potential together
concept_sections.explanation: Field points 'downhill' in potential: $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dx}$. In a uniform field the relationship is simply $V = Ed$, where $d$ is the distance along the field. So field (N/C) and potential-per-distance (V/m) are the same unit.

figure.caption: In a uniform field, equipotentials (dashed) are perpendicular to $\vec E$, and $V = Ed$.

concept_sections.heading: Equipotentials and the electron-volt
concept_sections.explanation: An equipotential is a surface of constant $V$; no work is done moving along it, and field lines cross it at right angles. Every point of a conductor in equilibrium is at the same potential. A handy energy unit is the electron-volt: $1\ \text{eV} = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ J, the energy an electron gains crossing 1 volt.

figure.caption: Field lines cross equipotential surfaces (dashed) at right angles.

real_world_examples.title: A 12-volt car battery
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: It maintains a potential difference $\Delta V = 12$ V; each coulomb of charge it pushes around the circuit gains $W = q\,\Delta V$ of energy to run lights and motors.

figure.caption: The battery holds a 12 V difference; each coulomb gains $W = q\,\Delta V$ driving the lamp.

real_world_examples.title: Defibrillator
real_world_examples.scenario: Paddles deliver a controlled shock to the heart.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A capacitor charged to a high potential dumps energy $U=qV$ through the chest, timed to reset the heart's rhythm.

figure.caption: A charged capacitor releases energy $U = qV$ through the chest to reset the heartbeat.

real_world_examples.title: Old TV / oscilloscope tube
real_world_examples.scenario: Electrons are accelerated toward a screen.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A potential difference does work $qV = \tfrac12 mv^2$, giving electrons a precise speed before they strike the phosphor.

figure.caption: A potential difference does work $qV = \tfrac12 mv^2$, setting the electron's speed before it hits the screen.

problems.prompt: Find the potential $0.30$ m from a $+5.0\ \mu\text{C}$ point charge.
problems.hint: Potential of a point charge is $kq/r$ (no square).

problems.prompt: How much work moves a $2.0\ \mu\text{C}$ charge through a potential difference of $100$ V?
problems.hint: Work equals charge times potential difference.

problems.prompt: A $3.0\ \mu\text{C}$ charge sits where the potential is $200$ V. Find its potential energy.
A uniform field $E = 5000$ N/C exists across a $2.0$ cm gap. Find the potential difference across the gap.
problems.hint: In a uniform field, voltage is field times distance.

problems.prompt: An electron is accelerated from rest through $100$ V. Find its final speed.
problems.hint: Set the energy gained $eV$ equal to kinetic energy.

problems.prompt: A $+3\ \mu\text{C}$ and a $-3\ \mu\text{C}$ charge are each $0.20$ m from point P. Find the potential at P.
solution_steps: Potentials add as scalars: $V = k\dfrac{+3\times10^{-6}}{0.20} + k\dfrac{-3\times10^{-6}}{0.20}$.
The two terms are equal and opposite.
problems.hint: Potential is a signed scalar; opposite equal charges at equal distance cancel.

problems.prompt: How much energy (in joules) does an electron gain crossing $500$ V?
problems.hint: Use $W = eV$; each volt gives the electron $1.6\times10^{-19}$ J.

problems.prompt: Two $+2.0\ \mu\text{C}$ charges are $0.40$ m apart. Find the potential at the midpoint between them.
solution_steps: Each charge is $0.20$ m from the midpoint.
problems.hint: Add the (scalar) potentials of the two charges — they reinforce here.

problems.prompt: Find the potential energy of a $+4.0\ \mu\text{C}$ and a $+2.0\ \mu\text{C}$ charge separated by $0.30$ m.
problems.hint: Use the pair potential energy $U = kq_1q_2/r$ (one power of $r$).

problems.prompt: How much work is required to bring two $+3.0\ \mu\text{C}$ charges from far apart to $0.10$ m apart?
solution_steps: Work equals the final potential energy (starting energy at infinity is zero).
problems.hint: The work done equals the assembled pair's potential energy.
